design_detail: Retrospective review of a prospectively collected clinical database, which the authors call an observational case series, at one Australian tertiary toxicology unit (Calvary Mater Newcastle, serving a population of over 300,000): every admission after an overdose of more than 400 mg of tramadol (above the maximum daily dose) from November 2000 to June 2013, whatever else was taken. 71 admissions in 70 patients; 20 took tramadol only and 51 took other medicines as well. There is no comparison group of other overdoses; within the series, the reported amount is compared between patients with and without seizures and with and without respiratory depression, and tramadol-only admissions are compared with admissions after co-ingestion.
can_establish: How often seizures, reduced consciousness, low oxygen saturation, fast heart rate, raised blood pressure, vomiting, intensive care and serotonin toxicity by the Hunter criteria occurred among 71 hospital admissions after tramadol overdoses of more than 400 mg at one Australian unit in 2000–2013, and that patients who had seizures or respiratory depression had reported taking larger amounts.
cannot_establish: The risk for a person who takes tramadol (the denominator is hospital admissions, not people using it); how much of each effect tramadol alone caused (51 of 71 took other medicines, and coma and respiratory depression are not reported separately for the 20 who took tramadol only); an amount below which seizures do not happen (amounts are self-reported and were not confirmed by laboratory tests, and only 8 people had seizures); serotonin toxicity at therapeutic doses or with antidepressants taken as prescribed (no such patients were studied); or effects rarer than about 1 in 20 overdoses (0 of 71 is compatible with up to 5.1%, editors' calculation).

sample.recruitment: Clinic. All overdose presentations to the toxicology service are recruited prospectively on a preformatted admission sheet and entered into a relational database within a week by trained research staff; this study selected from the database the tramadol overdoses of more than 400 mg admitted from November 2000 to June 2013 (PDF p. 2, Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: ingestion of more than 400 mg of tramadol, confirmed from the patient's history and collateral history recorded by ambulance, emergency and mental health staff, irrespective of co-ingestants. Of 112 tramadol overdose admissions, 16 were excluded because the amount was unknown and 25 because less than 400 mg was taken (PDF p. 2, Methods, 3rd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Median age 41 years (IQR 28–47, range 17–69); 43 of 71 (61%) female. Median reported tramadol amount 1000 mg (IQR 800–2000, range 450–6000); slow-release formulation in 22 of 71 (31%). Tramadol only: 20 (10 men, 10 women; median age 34). With other medicines: 51 (18 men, 33 women; median age 41) (PDF p. 2, Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2, PDF p. 3). Intent of the overdose is not reported.
sample.attrition: No loss during admission; no follow-up after discharge (a stated limitation, PDF p. 5). One patient contributed two admissions; results are reported per admission but called patients.
sample.selection_effects: Admissions to one specialist unit only: people who took tramadol and did not come to hospital, or were treated elsewhere, are not represented. Most (51 of 71) also took other medicines, among them benzodiazepines (16), SSRIs (13), SNRIs (10) and tricyclic antidepressants (3) (Table 1, PDF p. 3). Admissions with an unknown amount were excluded, and 3 of those 16 had seizures (PDF p. 3), so the seizure frequency and the amount comparison leave some seizures out.

exposure.measurement: Patient history and collateral history; the drugs reported were not routinely confirmed by laboratory analysis (a stated limitation, PDF p. 5). The authors cite earlier work from their unit as showing that the reported drug is accurate and the reported amount a good estimate of the amount taken (PDF p. 5, Discussion, 8th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: A single overdose; route not stated (the paper discusses oral formulations). Reported amounts, as study conditions: median 1000 mg (IQR 800–2000; range 450–6000); slow-release formulation in 22 of 71 admissions. Regular tramadol use before the overdose is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: 51 of 71 took other medicines (Table 1: tricyclic antidepressant 3, benzodiazepine 16, SSRI 13, SNRI 10, anti-serotonergic 2, other sedative 3, other 23; some took more than one). Table 2 compares tramadol-only and co-ingestion admissions for seizures (2 of 20, 10%, vs 6 of 51, 12%), gastrointestinal symptoms, ICU admission (0 vs 8) and intubation (0 vs 4), but not for coma or respiratory depression. Effects attributed to co-ingestants are named in the text (5 of the 8 ICU admissions). Alcohol is not mentioned.

comparison.controls: No external comparison group. Internal comparisons only: reported amount in patients with versus without seizures and with versus without respiratory depression (Mann–Whitney tests), and tramadol-only versus co-ingestion admissions (Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Epilepsy or earlier seizures, regular tramadol or other drug use, alcohol use, psychiatric history and CYP2D6 metabolizer status are not reported for the series; predisposing factors are described only for the two seizure patients who took the lowest amounts (benzodiazepine withdrawal; an earlier seizure unrelated to overdose).

outcomes.instruments: Pre-defined outcomes recorded on the preformatted admission sheet: (1) seizures; (2) serotonin toxicity by the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria (spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, sweating, tremor, hyperreflexia); (3) coma, GCS below 9; (4) respiratory depression, oxygen saturation below 94% and/or respiratory rate below 12 per minute, with time to onset; (5) ICU admission; (6) mechanical ventilation; (7) naloxone and response; (8) death. Also recorded: gastrointestinal effects, tachycardia (threshold not stated), mild hypertension (systolic above 140 mmHg), length of stay and time to first seizure (PDF p. 2, Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs; PDF p. 3, Results).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors describe the Hunter criteria as sensitive and specific (PDF p. 3, Discussion, 1st paragraph); the criteria come from the same research group (ref. 22). How seizures were ascertained and what counted as tachycardia are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm was the occurrence of each listed event during the admission. Coma and respiratory depression were derived from recorded observations (GCS, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation); naloxone response and time to respiratory depression were taken retrospectively from the medical record (PDF p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eight pre-defined outcomes are reported descriptively; the formal tests are two Mann–Whitney comparisons of the reported amount (seizures, respiratory depression), and the tramadol-only and co-ingestion groups are said not to differ in seizures, gastrointestinal symptoms and seizure amount without a named test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Database entry by trained research staff described as blinded to the outcomes of this study; serotonin toxicity was diagnosed prospectively against database definitions; treating clinicians were not blinded (PDF pp. 2, 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions of 71 admissions, with editors' exact 95% intervals in brackets: seizures 8 (11%; 5.0–21.0%); GCS below 15, 29 (41%; 29.3–53.2%); GCS below 9, 5 (7%; 2.3–15.7%); respiratory depression 13 (18%; 10.1–29.3%); tachycardia 27 (38%); systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg 32 (45%); vomiting 31 and nausea alone 5 (51%); ICU 8 (11%), all after co-ingestion; serotonin toxicity 0 (0–5.1%); deaths 0. Reported amount with versus without seizures: median 2100 mg (IQR 1600–3250) vs 1000 mg (IQR 775–1550), p=0.018 in the text and 0.021 in the Figure 1 legend. With versus without respiratory depression: median 2500 mg (IQR 1600–3000) vs 1000 mg (IQR 750–1475), p=0.003. Benzodiazepine co-ingestion: 1 of 8 with seizures (12.5%) vs 16 of 63 without (25%), not tested by the authors; editors' Fisher exact test p=0.67 (odds ratio 0.42).
analysis.covariates: None. All comparisons are unadjusted; co-ingestants, formulation and seizure history were not taken into account.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 compares tramadol-only and co-ingestion admissions for seizures, ICU and intubation but leaves out coma and respiratory depression, so the number of tramadol-only patients with respiratory depression is not given, although the Discussion says it occurred with tramadol alone (PDF p. 5). The comparison of amount by GCS is shown only as a figure, without a test (Figure 3, PDF p. 4). No confidence interval is given for any proportion.
analysis.power: Not reported. The amount comparisons rest on 8 seizures and 13 cases of respiratory depression. The absence of serotonin toxicity in 71 admissions rules out, at 95% confidence, a frequency above about 5% in such overdoses (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 71 admissions after tramadol overdoses above 400 mg (median reported 1000 mg), 11% had seizures, 18% low oxygen saturation, 41% some reduction in consciousness and 7% coma (three of the five after tricyclic antidepressants); fast heart rate and raised systolic blood pressure were common; no patient met the Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity, including patients who had also taken SSRIs (13) or SNRIs (10); nobody died. Patients with seizures or respiratory depression had reported larger amounts. The six seizures in patients without a predisposition followed reported amounts of 2000 mg or more; the two after 750 and 1200 mg had predisposing reasons.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says tramadol overdose 'causes' seizures and respiratory depression, a causal verb for an uncontrolled series in which 51 of 71 took other medicines; the abstract conclusion says 'is associated with'. The final paragraph extends the absence of serotonin toxicity in overdose to therapeutic use, "in therapeutic doses tramadol is unlikely to cause more than minor serotonergic effects" (PDF p. 5), although no patient taking therapeutic doses, alone or with prescribed antidepressants, was studied, and the case reports of serotonin toxicity the authors cite involve such combinations (PDF p. 4). The Discussion suggests benzodiazepines may lower the risk of seizures (PDF p. 5) from 1 of 8 vs 16 of 63, which the authors did not test (editors' Fisher exact p=0.67). It also says seizures occurred only above 2000 mg in patients without a predisposition (PDF p. 4), while the Results say 2000 mg or more (PDF p. 3). The comparisons with venlafaxine (seizures in about 5% of overdoses) and SSRIs (serotonin toxicity in about 15%) come from other studies, not from this series (PDF pp. 4–5). The frequencies themselves are reported faithfully in the abstract.

timeline.event: Spiller et al., prospective multicentre evaluation of tramadol exposures reported to US poison centres: seizures in 8%, as cited here (PDF p. 4); the authors cite it, with Shadnia et al. (2008), as also finding seizures at higher amounts
Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria published by the same research group; used here as the case definition of serotonin toxicity (ref. 22)
Marquardt et al., tramadol exposures reported to a statewide US poison control system: seizures in 14%, with fewer patients with coma and respiratory depression than here, as cited (PDF pp. 4–5)
Thundiyil et al.: tramadol accounted for 29 of 386 drug-overdose seizures (7.5%) logged by the California Poison Control System in 2003, as cited (PDF p. 4)

Talaie et al., Tehran poison centre (with Shadnia et al., 2008, from the same centre in a similar period): seizures in 46% and 35%; Talaie found no relation between amount and seizures, most seizures occurring after 500–1000 mg; the authors suggest the Tehran patients were selected for seizures (PDF pp. 4–5)
Rostam-Abadi et al., meta-analysis of Iranian series: seizures in a pooled 34.6% (95% CI 29.6–39.8) of 23 series of tramadol-poisoning admissions, prediction interval 12.5–60.9%

replication.where_it_stands: Seizures after tramadol overdose are reported in every series, but how often differs by setting: 8–14% in the US and Australian series, including this one, against 35–46% in the Tehran series and a pooled 34.6% in Iran. A relation between amount and seizures is found here and, as the authors report, by Spiller et al. and Shadnia et al., but not by Talaie et al. The absence of serotonin toxicity after tramadol overdose rests on this single series of 71 admissions; it says nothing about therapeutic combinations with antidepressants.

funding.funder: Nicole Ryan: NHMRC Early Career Fellowship Award ID 1072056. Geoff Isbister: NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship ID 1061041 (PDF p. 5, Funding sources).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no declarations of interest (PDF p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors work in the Department of Clinical Toxicology and Pharmacology, Calvary Mater Newcastle, and the University of Newcastle, the unit whose database was used; the Hunter criteria used for the diagnosis of serotonin toxicity were developed by the same group. Recorded as context for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A multicentre prospective cohort of tramadol overdoses in several countries, with tramadol and O-desmethyltramadol blood concentrations, laboratory confirmation of co-ingestants, standardized seizure and Hunter assessments by assessors blind to the amount, and enough patients who took tramadol alone to model the risk of seizures and respiratory depression by measured concentration; and, for serotonin toxicity, a cohort of people prescribed tramadol together with serotonergic antidepressants.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All admissions to one tertiary toxicology unit after tramadol overdoses above 400 mg over 13 years; suited to describing hospital overdoses, but one Australian centre, admitted patients only.
Every overdose presentation is recruited prospectively into the unit's database; all eligible admissions were taken.

71 admissions give seizures 11% with an exact 95% interval of 5.0–21.0% and exclude serotonin toxicity above about 5% (editors' calculation); too few events for the amount thresholds the Discussion draws.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, amount, formulation and co-ingestants are given (Results; Tables 1 and 2).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 41 of 112 admissions were excluded (unknown amount 16, under 400 mg 25), and 3 of the 16 excluded for an unknown amount had seizures; no follow-up after discharge.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Pre-defined outcomes and validated Hunter criteria, with stated thresholds for coma and respiratory depression; seizure ascertainment and tachycardia are not defined, and ingestion was not confirmed by laboratory analysis.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Preformatted admission sheet and prospective database entry by trained staff blinded to the study outcomes; naloxone response and time to respiratory depression were extracted retrospectively from records.

Medians and Mann–Whitney tests suit the data, but no interval accompanies any proportion, nothing is adjusted for co-ingestion, two different p-values are printed for the seizure comparison, and the benzodiazepine association is asserted without a test.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Record-based study with an ethics exemption; no participation was required.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI checklist has no overall algorithm; the editors summarize the risk of bias as moderate. Case capture was complete and prospective, and outcomes were pre-defined and recorded by staff blinded to this study's aims; the weaknesses are one centre, self-reported amounts without laboratory confirmation, co-ingestion in 72% of admissions that is not separated for coma and respiratory depression, the exclusion of unknown-amount admissions (which included seizures) and very few events for the amount comparisons. The card may be cited for the frequency of seizures, reduced consciousness, low oxygen saturation, adrenergic effects and intensive care, and for the absence of Hunter-defined serotonin toxicity (upper bound about 5%), among hospital admissions after tramadol overdoses above 400 mg in this Australian unit; not for the risk to a person taking tramadol, not for a safe amount, and not for serotonin toxicity at therapeutic doses.

key_findings.finding: 112 admissions for tramadol overdose from November 2000 to June 2013; 16 with an unknown amount and 25 with less than 400 mg were excluded, leaving 71 admissions in 70 patients: median age 41 years (IQR 28–47, range 17–69), 43 (61%) female, median reported amount 1000 mg (IQR 800–2000, range 450–6000), slow-release formulation in 22 (31%). 20 took tramadol only and 51 took other medicines as well.
Other medicines taken with tramadol (some patients took several): tricyclic antidepressant 3, benzodiazepine 16, SSRI 13, SNRI 10, anti-serotonergic 2, other sedative 3, other 23.

Seizures occurred in 8 of 71 (11%); one patient who took 4000 mg had six seizures. Median reported amount 2100 mg (IQR 1600–3250, range 750–4000) with seizures vs 1000 mg (IQR 775–1550, range 450–6000) without, p=0.018 (Mann–Whitney). The patient who had a seizure after 750 mg also had benzodiazepine withdrawal and the one after 1200 mg had had an earlier seizure unrelated to overdose; the other 6 took 2000 mg or more. Seizures also occurred in 3 of the 16 excluded admissions with an unknown amount.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical effects, 1st paragraph (starting p. 2, continuing p. 3); Figure 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The Figure 1 legend prints p=0.021. Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi: the six seizures without a predisposition were after about 2000, 2000, 2200, 3000, 3500 and 4000 mg, which reproduces the printed median of 2100 mg and IQR of 1600–3250 mg; at least two were at 2000 mg, not above it.

key_findings.finding: Median time from ingestion to the first seizure 8.5 hours (1.5–22.7): 1.5–11 hours after the immediate-release and 6.5–22.7 hours after the slow-release formulation.
key_findings.note: The bracket after 8.5 hours is not labelled; it matches the range of the two formulation groups. Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi: 3 seizures followed the immediate-release and 5 the slow-release formulation; the paper does not report seizure frequency by formulation.

key_findings.finding: No admission met the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; one patient who took 1000 mg of tramadol with 800 mg of escitalopram developed ocular clonus without meeting the criteria.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the exact 95% interval for 0 of 71 is 0–5.1%.

key_findings.finding: GCS below 15 in 29 of 71 (41%) and below 9 in 5: three after tricyclic antidepressants (GCS 3, 5 and 7) and two after 3000 mg and 900 mg of tramadol, both with respiratory depression that responded to naloxone. Respiratory depression with oxygen saturation below 94% in 13 (18%); median reported amount 2500 mg (IQR 1600–3000, range 500–4000) vs 1000 mg (IQR 750–1475, range 450–6000) without, p=0.003. Onset known in 9 of 13: within 2 hours in 7, at 5 and 8 hours in the other 2.
key_findings.note: Figure 4 (p. 4): 5 of the 13 with respiratory depression had co-ingested a tricyclic antidepressant (3) or promethazine (1) or had pneumonia (1). The abstract calls the two coma patients without tricyclics 'tramadol alone' (p. 1); the Results do not say so.

key_findings.finding: Gastrointestinal effects in 36 (51%): vomiting 31, nausea alone 5. Tachycardia in 27 (38%) and mild hypertension (systolic above 140 mmHg) in 32 (45%); one patient had a pre-existing left bundle branch block.

Median length of stay 16 hours (IQR 11.3–24.4, range 1.8–228); 19.9 hours (IQR 13.6–35.7) after co-ingestion. 8 patients (11%), all of whom had taken other medicines, went to intensive care: 5 for co-ingestant toxicity (tricyclic antidepressants 3, morphine 1, atenolol 1) and 3 for respiratory depression (one intubated, one on a naloxone infusion, one with pneumonia). No deaths. Naloxone was given to 9 patients, 7 with documented respiratory depression; it improved oxygen saturation or consciousness in 6, partly in 2 and not in 1; no seizures were reported after naloxone.

Tramadol only (n=20) vs tramadol with other medicines (n=51): seizures 2 (10%) vs 6 (12%); median amount with seizures 2100 vs 2100 mg; serotonin toxicity 0 vs 0; gastrointestinal symptoms 10 vs 26; ICU 0 vs 8; intubated or ventilated 0 vs 4; median length of stay 13.5 vs 19.9 hours; median maximum heart rate 96 vs 95; median maximum systolic pressure 137 vs 138 mmHg. Seizures, gastrointestinal symptoms and seizure amount were said not to differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Outcomes and treatment, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Patients who had co-ingested a benzodiazepine: 1 of 8 with seizures (12.5%) vs 16 of 63 without (25%); the Discussion takes this to suggest benzodiazepines may decrease the risk of seizures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical effects, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: No test is reported. Editors' Fisher exact test: p=0.67, odds ratio 0.42.

key_findings.finding: Figures the authors cite from other studies: seizures in 8% (Spiller et al.) and 14% (Marquardt et al.) of tramadol overdoses and in 35% and 46% in two Tehran poison-centre studies; seizures in about 5% of venlafaxine overdoses; serotonin toxicity in about 15% of SSRI overdoses; lower rates of coma (5–23%) and respiratory depression or dyspnoea (2–11%) in previous tramadol studies.

Stated limitations: retrospective design, possibly inaccurate reported amounts, drugs not routinely confirmed by laboratory analysis, and no follow-up after discharge; data were entered prospectively on a preformatted admission sheet.

reporting_issues.issue: The amount comparison between patients with and without seizures is given p=0.018 in the Results (p. 3) and p=0.021 in the Figure 1 legend (p. 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the direction is unaffected, but one of the two values is a transcription error.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists 16 patients who co-ingested a benzodiazepine, but the Results count 1 of 8 seizure patients plus 16 of 63 other patients, which makes 17.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two counts is wrong; the benzodiazepine comparison, already untested, cannot be reproduced exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says seizures occurred only with doses greater than 2000 mg in patients without a pre-existing risk (p. 4); the Results say 2000 mg or higher (p. 3), and Figure 1 shows at least two such seizures at about 2000 mg.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion's wording overstates the threshold; with six such seizures, no threshold can be inferred in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: Coma and respiratory depression are not reported separately for the 20 tramadol-only admissions (Table 2 omits them), although the Discussion says respiratory depression occurred in patients taking only tramadol (p. 5) and the abstract calls the two coma patients without tricyclics 'tramadol alone' (p. 1), which the Results do not state.
reporting_issues.consequence: How often tramadol alone was followed by coma or respiratory depression cannot be taken from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Respiratory depression is defined in the Methods as oxygen saturation below 94% and/or respiratory rate below 12 per minute (p. 2), but the Results report respiratory depression with oxygen saturation below 94% only (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether a slow breathing rate alone was counted; the 13 cases may be a saturation-based count.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods announce 'seven major outcomes' and then list eight (death is the eighth); tachycardia has no stated threshold; the bracket after the median time to first seizure is not labelled; the Discussion's one-fifth with respiratory depression is 18% in the Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor reporting slips; none changes a number a claim would cite, but the tachycardia figure (38%) cannot be compared with other series without a definition.

verification.source_read: PDF of the Early Online version (Clinical Toxicology 2015, Early Online: 1–6), not the version of record (53(6), 545–550); anchors give its own pages as PDF p. 1–6, which differ from the printed pages of the issue. All six pages read; Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 1–4 checked on 150-dpi renderings, Figures 1, 2 and 4 also at 300 dpi; no supplement.
